name: Ezekiel
v: The word of the LORD hit me:
Son of man, two women — daughters of the same mother.
They sold themselves in Egypt. Sold themselves young. There their breasts were handled, their virgin nipples fondled.
The older was Oholah. Her sister, Oholibah. They became mine. They bore me sons and daughters. As for their names: Oholah is Samaria. Oholibah is Jerusalem.
Oholah played the whore on me. She burned for her lovers — the Assyrians, the warriors next door —
dressed in royal blue, governors and commanders, every one of them a beautiful young man, every one of them a horseman.
She gave her body to all of them, the elite of Assyria. Every man she wanted, she defiled herself with him — and with all their filthy idols too.
She never let go of the whoring she started in Egypt. Men had taken her in her youth, mauled her virgin breasts, poured their lust into her — and she stayed in it.
So I handed her over. Handed her to the lovers she craved — to Assyria, the ones she burned for.
They stripped her naked. Took her sons and daughters. Killed her with the sword. She became a cautionary tale among women — judgment had been carried out.
Her sister Oholibah watched all this. And then went worse. Her lust was more depraved than her sister's, her whoring more reckless.
She too burned for the Assyrians — governors and commanders, soldiers in full uniform, horsemen, every one of them a beautiful young man.
I saw it. She had defiled herself the same way. The two sisters walked the same road.
But she pushed further. She saw men carved on a wall — figures of Chaldeans etched in red,
belts at their waists, flowing turbans on their heads, every one of them looking like an officer, looking like Babylon — Chaldea, their birthplace.
One look and she was on fire for them. She sent messengers to them in Chaldea.
So the Babylonians came to her, came to her bed of love, and defiled her with their lust. And after they had used her — she turned from them in disgust.
When her whoring went public, when she exposed herself for all to see, I turned from her in disgust, the way I had turned from her sister.
But she only multiplied her whoring, remembering her girlhood in Egypt, when she sold herself there.
She lusted after their gigolos — men hung like donkeys, men who came like horses.
You went back to the obscenity of your youth — back to Egypt, where they handled your young breasts, where they fondled the breasts of a girl.
So this is what the Lord GOD says, Oholibah: I am going to wake up your lovers against you — the very ones you turned from in disgust. I will bring them against you from every side —
the Babylonians and all the Chaldeans, Pekod and Shoa and Koa, and all the Assyrians with them — beautiful young men, governors and commanders, officers and warriors, every one of them riding.

They will come at you with weapons, with chariots and wagons and a horde of nations. Shields and helmets and armor will close in on you from every direction. I will hand you over for judgment, and they will judge you by their own laws.

I will turn my jealousy loose on you. They will deal with you in fury — cut off your nose and your ears, kill what is left of you with the sword. They will take your sons and daughters, and what remains will burn.
They will strip the clothes off you and take your jewelry.
That is how I will put an end to your obscenity, to the whoring you brought from Egypt. You will never look back at it again. You will never remember Egypt again.
For this is what the Lord GOD says: I am about to hand you over to those you hate — to those you turned from in disgust.
They will treat you with hatred. They will take everything you worked for and leave you naked and bare. The shame of your whoring will be exposed — the obscenity, the lust —
this is what your whoring has earned you. Because you ran after the nations, because you defiled yourself with their idols.
You walked your sister's road. So I am putting her cup in your hand.

This is what the Lord GOD says:

You will drink your sister's cup —
deep and wide,
brimming with mockery and contempt,
holding more than you can hold.

You will fill up with drunkenness and grief —
a cup of horror and devastation —
the cup of your sister Samaria.

You will drink it. Drain it.
Chew on the broken shards.
Tear at your own breasts.

I have spoken. The declaration of the Lord GOD.
So this is what the Lord GOD says: Because you forgot me, because you threw me behind your back — you carry the weight of your obscenity, you carry the weight of your whoring.
The LORD said to me: Son of man, will you judge Oholah and Oholibah? Then confront them with their atrocities.
They have committed adultery. Blood is on their hands. They committed adultery with their idols. The children they bore me — they made them pass through the fire, food for those things.
And there is more. They defiled my sanctuary on the same day. Trampled my Sabbaths.
After slaughtering their children to their idols, they walked into my sanctuary the same day to desecrate it. Inside my own house — that is what they did.
More than that — they sent for men to come from far away. Messengers were dispatched, and the men came. And for them, you bathed. You painted your eyes. You put on your jewelry.
You stretched out on a luxurious couch with a table laid before it — and on that table you set my incense and my oil.
Around her, the noise of a careless crowd — drunkards hauled in from the desert. They put bracelets on the sisters' wrists and crowns of beauty on their heads.
And I said of the one worn out by adultery: now they will whore with her, and she with them.
They went in to her — the way a man goes in to a prostitute. That is how they went in to Oholah and Oholibah, women of obscenity.

But righteous men will pass sentence on them — the sentence given to adulteresses, the sentence given to women who shed blood. Because that is what they are. Adulteresses. Murderers. Blood on their hands.
This is what the Lord GOD says: Bring up an army against them. Hand them over to terror and plunder.
The army will stone them, cut them down with swords, slaughter their sons and daughters, burn their houses to the ground.
That is how I will purge this obscenity from the land — a warning to every woman not to imitate it.
They will pay for their obscenity. They will carry the consequences of their idol-worship. And then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.

com.d:
# Ezekiel 23: The Weight of Unfaithfulness

The Spirit of God uses one of Scripture's most jarring metaphors—two sisters engaged in spiritual adultery—to break through Israel's stubborn refusal to see how far they have wandered from covenant love. This chapter confronts us with a painful truth: unfaithfulness to God carries devastating consequences, not because He is vengeful, but because He loves His people enough to let them experience the fruit of their own choices.

Ezekiel presents Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem) as sisters who, despite having been chosen and loved by God, prostitute themselves to foreign powers and false gods. The language is explicit and uncomfortable—deliberately so. God isn't being crude; He's using imagery that mirrors the raw betrayal a spouse experiences when trust is shattered. This is the language of heartbreak, and it reveals something crucial: our covenant with God is personal. It matters. Our turning away wounds Him because relationship is at stake, not merely religious compliance.

What makes this passage particularly searching is that it shows how subtle spiritual unfaithfulness can become. The sisters didn't abandon God openly at first; they gradually entangled themselves with foreign alliances and practices, allowing compromise to become conviction. They gave their hearts elsewhere while maintaining the appearance of faithfulness. Sound familiar? We do the same when we chase security in money, approval in status, or comfort in addictions while still calling ourselves His.

Yet even in this severe word lies an implicit plea: repent. God's graphic descriptions are meant to awaken, not destroy. He exposes our patterns because He wants us to see them and turn back toward Him.

Consider: What compromises have you rationalized as merely practical or harmless? Where are you dividing your heart's allegiance between God and something else?
com.s:
Ezekiel 23 presents one of the most provocative and disturbing allegories in the Hebrew Bible, employing graphic sexual imagery to depict the covenant unfaithfulness of Israel and Judah. The chapter belongs to a series of judgment oracles delivered during the Babylonian exile, likely composed between 593 and 571 BCE, when Ezekiel ministered among the Judean deportees at Tel-abib. This extended metaphor builds upon the earlier allegory in chapter 16 while introducing the distinctive feature of two sisters representing the divided kingdoms.

The sisters bear symbolic names freighted with meaning: Oholah (*ʾohŏlāh*, "her tent") represents Samaria and the northern kingdom, while Oholibah (*ʾohŏlîḇāh*, "my tent is in her") signifies Jerusalem and Judah. These names carry cultic significance, with Oholah's "tent" possibly alluding to illegitimate worship sanctuaries, while Oholibah's name pointedly references Yahweh's dwelling presence in Jerusalem's temple. The allegory traces their "prostitution" (*zənûnîm*) beginning in Egypt, employing this term not merely for sexual immorality but as a comprehensive metaphor for political alliances and religious syncretism that violated covenant exclusivity.

The literary structure moves systematically from Oholah's judgment through Assyrian conquest to Oholibah's even greater culpability. The younger sister witnessed her sibling's destruction yet pursued the same diplomatic entanglements with Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt, depicted through increasingly explicit imagery that has generated substantial interpretive discomfort among commentators. Feminist scholars have rightly raised concerns about the chapter's violent rhetoric and its potential to normalize abuse, while traditional interpreters emphasize the prophetic function of shock rhetoric to convey the severity of covenant betrayal.

The Hebrew term *šāpaṭ* ("to judge") appears prominently, indicating that the foreign nations serve paradoxically as instruments of divine justice against the very peoples with whom Israel and Judah sought alliance. The cup of judgment motif in verses 31–34 connects this passage to broader prophetic traditions and anticipates similar imagery in Revelation. Within Ezekiel's canonical placement, chapter 23 concludes a trilogy of allegories preparing for Jerusalem's fall, making theological sense of impending catastrophe while maintaining Yahweh's sovereign righteousness over covenant violations spanning generations.
com.p:
This sobering allegory was delivered through the prophet Ezekiel around 590 BC, during the Babylonian exile, approximately six centuries before the incarnation of Christ. The prophet speaks to a people already experiencing divine judgment—Jerusalem's final destruction still lay a few years ahead, but the exile had begun. Ezekiel's ministry stands at the devastating pivot point between the Kingdom era and the Exile, that painful severing when God's visible presence would depart from the temple and His covenant people would languish among the nations.

The passage presents Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, whose names carry theological freight: "her own tent" and "my tent is in her"—references to false worship versus the legitimate sanctuary. Both sisters are portrayed as unfaithful wives who pursued adulterous alliances with foreign powers, trusting in Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon rather than their covenant Lord. The graphic imagery, disturbing in its explicitness, reveals the depth of God's wounded love and the severity of spiritual adultery. What Israel did with pagan nations and their gods was not merely political miscalculation but marital betrayal against the Holy One who had chosen them from Egypt's womb.

Within redemptive history, this chapter exposes the utter failure of the old covenant arrangement—not because of any deficiency in God's faithfulness, but because of Israel's incurable heart condition. The law could diagnose sin but could not cure it. The prophets could expose treachery but could not transform affections. This unflinching portrait of covenant failure creates desperate longing for what Ezekiel himself would later promise: a new covenant, a new heart, God's own Spirit placed within His people.

The typological threads run toward Christ, the faithful Bridegroom who would succeed where Israel failed, who would endure the judgment His bride deserved. The cup of wrath that Oholibah must drink finds its ultimate expression in Gethsemane, where the Son asked if this cup might pass, then drank it to the dregs for His people. The harlot bride becomes the holy bride only through substitutionary love.

For the church awaiting Christ's return, this passage guards against presumption. Proximity to sacred things guarantees nothing—Oholibah had the temple yet proved more corrupt than her sister. The call remains: single-hearted devotion to the Bridegroom who purchased His bride with blood, trusting no alliance but His finished work.
